passages.title: Peace elsewhere does not answer Jerusalem's distress
passages.summary: In the second year of Darius, Zechariah calls the people to return to the LORD. Their fathers ignored the prophets, and the warnings came true. Then Zechariah sees a vision at night. A man on a red horse stands among myrtle trees with other riders. They have patrolled the earth and found it quiet. The LORD’s angel asks how long Jerusalem must go without mercy. God answers with kind and comforting words. He is angry with the nations that are at ease.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson connects returning to God with becoming holy. Why does the angel question the patrol’s report of peace?

contextNote.title: Peace elsewhere does not answer Jerusalem's distress
contextNote.text: The patrol reports in verse 11 that the whole earth is at rest. That sounds like good news. For Jerusalem it is not. The world is calm while the city still lies in ruins. In verse 12 an angel asks God, “how long?” Verse 15 says God is angry with the nations at ease. They went further in harming Judah than he intended.

passages.title: The measured city receives a promise larger than its walls
passages.summary: Zechariah sees a man with a measuring line going to measure Jerusalem. An angel sends word to stop him. Jerusalem will be like villages without walls, since so many will live there. The LORD will be a wall of fire around it. He calls the exiles to escape from Babylon. Whoever touches them touches the apple of his eye. He is coming to live among his people. Many nations will join themselves to the LORD and be his people.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson studies God dwelling among a people who become holy. How does the promise of protection change the meaning of the measuring line?

contextNote.title: The measured city receives a promise larger than its walls
contextNote.text: The man in verse 1 means to measure the city, perhaps for its walls. Verse 4 says the city will be too full for walls. Verse 5 gives a different protection: God himself as a wall of fire. Verse 11 then widens who lives inside. Many nations will join the LORD. He calls them “my people,” the name once given to Israel alone. The promise is larger than any line can mark.

passages.title: Changed clothing answers the accusation against the priest
passages.summary: Zechariah sees the high priest Joshua standing before the LORD’s angel. The accuser stands at his right hand. The LORD rebukes the accuser and calls Joshua a stick snatched from the fire. Joshua is wearing filthy clothes. The angel orders them removed and says his guilt is taken away. He is dressed in fine robes and a clean turban. He is told to walk in God’s ways. God promises to bring his servant, the Branch.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson uses Joshua’s changed clothing to discuss holiness and changed conduct. What must Joshua still do after receiving clean clothing?

contextNote.title: Changed clothing answers the accusation against the priest
contextNote.text: Verse 3 admits that Joshua’s clothes are filthy. The accuser has grounds. The reply in verse 2 does not claim Joshua is clean. It points to God’s choice of Jerusalem. Verse 4 then removes the clothes and the guilt together. Joshua does not change his own garments. Verse 7 gives him duties after the gift, not before it.

passages.title: The vision directs attention back to unfinished work
passages.summary: An angel wakes Zechariah and shows him a gold lampstand with seven lamps. Two olive trees stand beside it. The angel gives a word for Zerubbabel the governor. The work will be done by God’s Spirit, not by might or power. The great mountain before him will become level ground. His hands laid the temple’s foundation, and his hands will finish it. No one should despise the day of small things. The two olive trees are the two anointed ones.
passages.uncertainty: The vision names no securely mapped location for its objects. Symbolic movements receive no ordinary route.

lds.text: Why does the promise mention both laying the foundation and finishing the house?

contextNote.title: The vision directs attention back to unfinished work
contextNote.text: The vision is strange, and its message is practical. The temple’s foundation was laid, and then the work stalled (Ezra 4:24). Verse 6 says how it will be finished. The builders have no army or great strength. God’s Spirit will do it. Verse 9 promises that the hands that began will finish. Verse 10 speaks to those who scorned a small beginning.

passages.title: Wrongdoing leaves houses without their supposed protection
passages.summary: Zechariah sees a huge scroll flying through the air. It carries a curse over the whole land. It condemns everyone who steals and everyone who swears falsely. It will enter their houses and consume timber and stone. Then he sees a measuring basket with a lead cover. A woman sits inside, and she is called Wickedness. Two winged women lift the basket into the sky. They carry it away to the land of Babylon.
passages.uncertainty: The vision names no securely mapped location for its objects. Symbolic movements receive no ordinary route.

lds.text: What happens when the curse enters houses built to shelter their owners?

contextNote.title: Wrongdoing leaves houses without their supposed protection
contextNote.text: The scroll names two wrongs: theft and false oaths. One harms a neighbor, and the other misuses God’s name. Verse 4 says the curse goes into the offender’s house. A house is where people keep what they took and feel safe. The curse stays there and takes the building apart. So wrongdoing removes its own shelter. The second vision carries wickedness out of the land altogether.

passages.title: A crown links distant gifts with the temple's future
passages.summary: Zechariah sees four chariots come out between two bronze mountains. They go out to patrol the whole earth. Then God tells him to collect silver and gold from exiles newly come from Babylon. He must make a crown and set it on Joshua the high priest. He says a man called the Branch will build the LORD’s temple. That man will rule on his throne and be a priest there. The crown will be kept in the temple as a reminder. People from far away will come and help build.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Zechariah names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: How do gifts from distant people become part of the temple’s future?

contextNote.title: A crown links distant gifts with the temple's future
contextNote.text: The crown is set on a priest, not on the governor. Verse 13 then describes one figure called the Branch. He builds the temple, sits on a throne, and serves as priest. Israel had kept those two offices apart. Here there is “counsel of peace” between them. The gold comes from exiles who just arrived (verse 10). Verse 15 says more people from far away will share in the building.

passages.title: A question about fasting becomes a question about injured neighbors
passages.summary: Men come from Bethel to ask the priests a question. For years they have fasted in the fifth month. They ask whether they should continue. God asks whether their fasting was really for him. He recalls what the earlier prophets said. Judge fairly, and show kindness and mercy to one another. Do not oppress widows, orphans, foreigners, or the poor. The fathers refused to listen, and so they were scattered.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson connects holiness with compassion and protection for injured neighbors. Why does the answer move from fasting dates to injured neighbors?

contextNote.title: A question about fasting becomes a question about injured neighbors
contextNote.text: The fifth-month fast mourned the burning of the temple (2 Kings 25:8–9). God does not answer the question until 8:19. He first asks whom the fasting served (verses 5–6). Then verses 9–10 repeat the earlier prophets’ demand. Four groups are named: widows, orphans, foreigners, and the poor. Neglect of them led to the loss now being mourned. Grief over the loss means little if its cause continues.

passages.title: A restored city must be safe enough for ordinary life
passages.summary: The LORD says he is returning to Zion to live in Jerusalem. Old men and women will sit in its streets with their canes. The streets will be full of boys and girls playing. God will bring his people from east and west. He tells them to be strong and finish the temple. They must speak truth and judge fairly at their gates. The fasts will become glad feasts. Ten foreigners will take hold of one Jew’s robe and ask to go with him.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson studies truth and peace as part of a future holy community. What do playing children show about the city’s restored life?

contextNote.title: A restored city must be safe enough for ordinary life
contextNote.text: Verses 4–5 measure the restored city by two groups. Old people sit outside, and children play in the streets. These are the ages least able to defend themselves. No walls or soldiers are mentioned. A city is safe when they can use its streets. Verses 16–17 say what that takes: true speech and fair courts. Verse 19 finally answers the question about fasting from chapter 7.

passages.title: The promised king removes weapons while the chapter still contains battle
passages.summary: A message of judgment falls on Syria, Tyre, and the Philistine cities. God will guard his house against every army. Zion is told to rejoice, for her king is coming. He is righteous and humble and rides on a donkey. He will remove chariots, war horses, and bows from Israel. He will speak peace to the nations and rule from sea to sea. God will free the prisoners because of his covenant. He will save his people like a flock.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson reads the coming king through Matthew’s later account of Jesus entering Jerusalem. How does removing weapons explain the announced peace?

contextNote.title: The promised king removes weapons while the chapter still contains battle
contextNote.text: Verse 9 brings the king on a donkey, not a war horse. Verse 10 then says what he removes. The chariots of Ephraim and the horses of Jerusalem are Israel’s own. He disarms his own side. His rule spreads by speaking peace. Verses 13–15 still describe battle, and the chapter keeps both pictures. Matthew 21:5 quotes verse 9 about Jesus entering Jerusalem.

passages.title: Failed guidance leaves people scattered like an untended flock
passages.summary: The people are told to ask the LORD for rain in the spring. Household idols speak nonsense, and fortune-tellers see lies. Their comfort is empty. So the people wander like sheep with no shepherd. God is angry with the shepherds and will care for his flock himself. He will strengthen Judah and save the house of Joseph. He will whistle for them and gather them in. He will bring them home from Egypt and Assyria.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: How does failed guidance leave the people like untended sheep?

contextNote.title: Failed guidance leaves people scattered like an untended flock
contextNote.text: Verse 1 says to ask the LORD, who makes the storm clouds. Verse 2 names where the people have been asking. They turn to household idols, diviners, and dreamers. The comfort they receive is false. The verse then states a result in society. People drift like sheep and suffer because no one leads them. In verse 3 God answers by becoming their shepherd himself.

passages.title: Selling the flock turns care into profit
passages.summary: Zechariah is told to shepherd a flock marked for slaughter. Its buyers kill the sheep and feel no guilt. Its sellers thank God that they are rich. He takes two staffs, named Favor and Union. He grows weary of the flock, and they detest him. He breaks the staff Favor and asks for his wages. They weigh out thirty pieces of silver, and he throws it to the potter. He breaks the second staff, and a worthless shepherd follows.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson connects the weighed silver with Matthew’s later account concerning Judas. What happens when the people responsible for care treat the flock as profit?

contextNote.title: Selling the flock turns care into profit
contextNote.text: Verse 5 names three groups who gain from the flock. Buyers slaughter and go unpunished. Sellers say, “Blessed be the LORD, for I am rich.” The flock’s own shepherds feel no pity. Religious words cover the trade. The good shepherd’s pay in verse 12 is thirty pieces of silver. Exodus 21:32 sets that as the price of a slave.

passages.title: Rescue outside the city comes before the city's honor
passages.summary: The LORD will make Jerusalem a cup that makes the nations stagger. All who try to lift that heavy stone will hurt themselves. The clans of Judah will be like fire among sheaves. The LORD will save the tents of Judah first. David’s house and Jerusalem will not be honored above the rest. Then God will pour out a spirit of grace and prayer. They will look on one they pierced and mourn. Every family will mourn by itself.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson reads the pierced figure through John’s account and later Revelation. Why does rescue for the tents come before honor for the capital?

contextNote.title: Rescue outside the city comes before the city's honor
contextNote.text: Verse 7 sets an order for the rescue. The “tents of Judah,” the countryside, are saved first. The verse gives the reason. The capital and the royal house must not rise above the others. Verse 10 then turns victory into mourning. The leading families weep one by one (verses 12–14). John 19:37 applies verse 10 to the death of Jesus.

passages.title: Cleansing includes the collapse of false claims and the testing of survivors
passages.summary: On that day a fountain will be opened to cleanse sin. God will remove the names of the idols from the land. False prophets will be ashamed and deny their trade. A sword is called against God’s shepherd. The shepherd is struck, and the sheep scatter. Two thirds of the people will perish. The last third will pass through fire and be refined like silver. They will call on God, and he will call them his people.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson connects the struck shepherd with Matthew and the wounds with Restoration scripture. What does the final exchange say about the survivors’ relationship with God?

contextNote.title: Cleansing includes the collapse of false claims and the testing of survivors
contextNote.text: The chapter moves in four steps. A fountain cleanses (verse 1), and false prophecy ends (verses 2–6). The shepherd is struck (verse 7), and the survivors are refined (verses 8–9). Being among the survivors is not the end. Fire tests them as silver and gold are tested. Verse 9 closes with both sides speaking. God says, “It is my people,” and they say, “The LORD is my God.”

passages.title: Holiness reaches ordinary pots after a vision of terrible conflict
passages.summary: A day of the LORD is coming when nations will attack Jerusalem. The city will be taken, and half its people exiled. Then the LORD will fight, and his feet will stand on the Mount of Olives. Living water will flow from Jerusalem all year. The LORD will be king over all the earth. Survivors of the nations will come each year to worship him. Even the bells on the horses will be marked as holy. Every cooking pot in Jerusalem will be holy to the LORD.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. Visions and promises do not establish traveled army or return paths.

lds.text: The lesson uses daily objects to discuss holiness and gives later readings about Christ’s return. How does holiness on cooking pots change the final image of worship?

contextNote.title: Holiness reaches ordinary pots after a vision of terrible conflict
contextNote.text: The chapter begins with a city plundered (verse 2). It ends with kitchens. “Holy to the LORD” was engraved on the high priest’s gold plate (Exodus 28:36). Verse 20 puts those words on horses’ bells. Verse 21 makes every pot in the city fit for sacred use. The line between holy and common is removed by raising everything. Verse 16 includes survivors from the nations in the worship.

No walls or soldiers are mentioned. A city is safe when they can use its streets. Verses 16–17 say what that takes: true speech and fair courts. Verse 19 finally answers the question about fasting from chapter 7.

events.title: The promised king removes weapons while the chapter still contains battle
events.summary: A message of judgment falls on Syria, Tyre, and the Philistine cities. God will guard his house against every army. Zion is told to rejoice, for her king is coming. He is righteous and humble and rides on a donkey. He will remove chariots, war horses, and bows from Israel. He will speak peace to the nations and rule from sea to sea. God will free the prisoners because of his covenant. He will save his people like a flock.
events.detail: Verse 9 brings the king on a donkey, not a war horse. Verse 10 then says what he removes. The chariots of Ephraim and the horses of Jerusalem are Israel’s own. He disarms his own side. His rule spreads by speaking peace. Verses 13–15 still describe battle, and the chapter keeps both pictures. Matthew 21:5 quotes verse 9 about Jesus entering Jerusalem.

events.title: Failed guidance leaves people scattered like an untended flock
events.summary: The people are told to ask the LORD for rain in the spring. Household idols speak nonsense, and fortune-tellers see lies. Their comfort is empty. So the people wander like sheep with no shepherd. God is angry with the shepherds and will care for his flock himself. He will strengthen Judah and save the house of Joseph. He will whistle for them and gather them in. He will bring them home from Egypt and Assyria.
events.detail: Verse 1 says to ask the LORD, who makes the storm clouds. Verse 2 names where the people have been asking. They turn to household idols, diviners, and dreamers. The comfort they receive is false. The verse then states a result in society. People drift like sheep and suffer because no one leads them. In verse 3 God answers by becoming their shepherd himself.

events.title: Selling the flock turns care into profit
events.summary: Zechariah is told to shepherd a flock marked for slaughter. Its buyers kill the sheep and feel no guilt. Its sellers thank God that they are rich. He takes two staffs, named Favor and Union. He grows weary of the flock, and they detest him. He breaks the staff Favor and asks for his wages. They weigh out thirty pieces of silver, and he throws it to the potter. He breaks the second staff, and a worthless shepherd follows.
events.detail: Verse 5 names three groups who gain from the flock. Buyers slaughter and go unpunished. Sellers say, “Blessed be the LORD, for I am rich.” The flock’s own shepherds feel no pity. Religious words cover the trade. The good shepherd’s pay in verse 12 is thirty pieces of silver. Exodus 21:32 sets that as the price of a slave.

events.title: Rescue outside the city comes before the city's honor
events.summary: The LORD will make Jerusalem a cup that makes the nations stagger. All who try to lift that heavy stone will hurt themselves. The clans of Judah will be like fire among sheaves. The LORD will save the tents of Judah first. David’s house and Jerusalem will not be honored above the rest. Then God will pour out a spirit of grace and prayer. They will look on one they pierced and mourn. Every family will mourn by itself.
events.detail: Verse 7 sets an order for the rescue. The “tents of Judah,” the countryside, are saved first. The verse gives the reason. The capital and the royal house must not rise above the others. Verse 10 then turns victory into mourning. The leading families weep one by one (verses 12–14). John 19:37 applies verse 10 to the death of Jesus.

events.title: Cleansing includes the collapse of false claims and the testing of survivors
events.summary: On that day a fountain will be opened to cleanse sin. God will remove the names of the idols from the land. False prophets will be ashamed and deny their trade. A sword is called against God’s shepherd. The shepherd is struck, and the sheep scatter. Two thirds of the people will perish. The last third will pass through fire and be refined like silver. They will call on God, and he will call them his people.
events.detail: The chapter moves in four steps. A fountain cleanses (verse 1), and false prophecy ends (verses 2–6). The shepherd is struck (verse 7), and the survivors are refined (verses 8–9). Being among the survivors is not the end. Fire tests them as silver and gold are tested. Verse 9 closes with both sides speaking. God says, “It is my people,” and they say, “The LORD is my God.”

events.summary: A day of the LORD is coming when nations will attack Jerusalem. The city will be taken, and half its people exiled. Then the LORD will fight, and his feet will stand on the Mount of Olives. Living water will flow from Jerusalem all year. The LORD will be king over all the earth. Survivors of the nations will come each year to worship him. Even the bells on the horses will be marked as holy. Every cooking pot in Jerusalem will be holy to the LORD.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Persian royal road
ancientRoads.summary: Persian kings kept a road with rest stations from Sardis to Susa. Herodotus counted 111 stations on it.
ancientRoads.detail: Royal messengers changed horses at the stations. Esther 8:10 sends the king’s letters by riders on royal horses.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Herodotus names lands and rivers, not towns. The line between Sardis and Susa is a broad guide.

guides.title: Zechariah: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Changed clothing answers the accusation against the priest
steps.text: Verse 3 admits that Joshua’s clothes are filthy. The accuser has grounds. The reply in verse 2 does not claim Joshua is clean. It points to God’s choice of Jerusalem. Verse 4 then removes the clothes and the guilt together. Joshua does not change his own garments. Verse 7 gives him duties after the gift, not before it.

steps.title: A question about fasting becomes a question about injured neighbors
steps.text: The fifth-month fast mourned the burning of the temple (2 Kings 25:8–9). God does not answer the question until 8:19. He first asks whom the fasting served (verses 5–6). Then verses 9–10 repeat the earlier prophets’ demand. Four groups are named: widows, orphans, foreigners, and the poor. Neglect of them led to the loss now being mourned. Grief over the loss means little if its cause continues.

steps.title: The promised king removes weapons while the chapter still contains battle
steps.text: Verse 9 brings the king on a donkey, not a war horse. Verse 10 then says what he removes. The chariots of Ephraim and the horses of Jerusalem are Israel’s own. He disarms his own side. His rule spreads by speaking peace. Verses 13–15 still describe battle, and the chapter keeps both pictures. Matthew 21:5 quotes verse 9 about Jesus entering Jerusalem.

steps.title: Holiness reaches ordinary pots after a vision of terrible conflict
steps.text: The chapter begins with a city plundered (verse 2). It ends with kitchens. “Holy to the LORD” was engraved on the high priest’s gold plate (Exodus 28:36). Verse 20 puts those words on horses’ bells. Verse 21 makes every pot in the city fit for sacred use. The line between holy and common is removed by raising everything. Verse 16 includes survivors from the nations in the worship.

chapterMaps.narrative: In the second year of Darius, Zechariah calls the people to return to the LORD. Their fathers ignored the prophets, and the warnings came true. Then Zechariah sees a vision at night. A man on a red horse stands among myrtle trees with other riders. They have patrolled the earth and found it quiet. The LORD’s angel asks how long Jerusalem must go without mercy. God answers with kind and comforting words. He is angry with the nations that are at ease.

chapterMaps.narrative: Zechariah is told to shepherd a flock marked for slaughter. Its buyers kill the sheep and feel no guilt. Its sellers thank God that they are rich. He takes two staffs, named Favor and Union. He grows weary of the flock, and they detest him. He breaks the staff Favor and asks for his wages. They weigh out thirty pieces of silver, and he throws it to the potter. He breaks the second staff, and a worthless shepherd follows.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD will make Jerusalem a cup that makes the nations stagger. All who try to lift that heavy stone will hurt themselves. The clans of Judah will be like fire among sheaves. The LORD will save the tents of Judah first. David’s house and Jerusalem will not be honored above the rest. Then God will pour out a spirit of grace and prayer. They will look on one they pierced and mourn. Every family will mourn by itself.

chapterMaps.narrative: On that day a fountain will be opened to cleanse sin. God will remove the names of the idols from the land. False prophets will be ashamed and deny their trade. A sword is called against God’s shepherd. The shepherd is struck, and the sheep scatter. Two thirds of the people will perish. The last third will pass through fire and be refined like silver. They will call on God, and he will call them his people.

chapterMaps.narrative: A day of the LORD is coming when nations will attack Jerusalem. The city will be taken, and half its people exiled. Then the LORD will fight, and his feet will stand on the Mount of Olives. Living water will flow from Jerusalem all year. The LORD will be king over all the earth. Survivors of the nations will come each year to worship him. Even the bells on the horses will be marked as holy. Every cooking pot in Jerusalem will be holy to the LORD.

textRoutes.title: Men arrive from Babylon
textRoutes.summary: Three men have come from Babylon with silver and gold. Zechariah is to make crowns from it and crown Joshua the high priest.
